title: Free to download, impossible to hold
summary: Moonshot's Kimi K3 open weights arrive tomorrow — the largest open model ever at 2.8 trillion parameters, and a 1.4-terabyte download that takes roughly eighteen high-end accelerators just to load, so 'open' no longer means local. Then AREX, a deep-research agent that beats far larger models by exploiting a simple asymmetry: an answer is cheaper to check than to find. Plus a Sunday week-in-review on a cost week wearing a capability week's clothes.

topics: Kimi K3 open weights (Moonshot AI): full weights scheduled for July 27 2026, the largest open-weight model ever at 2.8 trillion parameters (~triple Kimi K2.6); shipped in MXFP4 four-bit quantization at ~1.4TB (~5.6TB in 16-bit); reporting (Techi) estimates ~18 80GB accelerators just to load the weights and that a single 8x192GB node (~1.5TB) can 'barely fit the weights with almost nothing to spare', so serving real traffic needs dozens of accelerators; MXFP4 runs natively on Nvidia Blackwell and AMD MI400 only; Modified MIT license; built on Kimi Delta Attention, Stable LatentMoE, 1M context; framing: open weights at this scale do not push capability to the edge, they move it to whoever can keep 1.4TB loaded and busy — most adopters will rent it via Moonshot's API or a cloud host; real value is price competition across hosts, data-residency/sovereignty, and researcher access to study the architecture

AREX (recursively self-improving deep-research agent): exploits the discovery-verification asymmetry — finding an answer that jointly satisfies many constraints is costly, but evaluating a candidate decomposes into simpler constraint-wise checks; built as an inner research loop plus an outer self-improvement loop that audits an answer constraint-by-constraint and accepts/refines-the-broken-piece/restarts, carrying verified progress forward via an autonomous context-update tool; AREX-Base is 122B total/10B active, AREX-Turbo 4B; authors report BrowseComp 82.5%, GAIA 85.4% (vs Gemini 3.1 Pro 80.6%), matching/beating much larger frontier models on several deep-research benchmarks while trailing on a hard closed-book QA set; ablations: removing the outer loop 82.5->69.8, removing autonomous context updating 82.5->71.4; all numbers authors' own, unreplicated, no downloadable tool

threads.name: AI sovereignty and open weights
threads.status: The week's policy fight (a reported US push to restrict Chinese open-weight models, a Treasury sanctions threat over alleged distillation, and a 25-company Microsoft-organized letter opposing broad restrictions) is overtaken by the artifact: Moonshot ships Kimi K3's open weights July 27 — the largest open model ever, 2.8T parameters — regardless of any policy decision. The show's dive reframed 'open' at this scale as non-local: a 1.4TB download needing ~18+ accelerators to load, so capability moves to whoever can host it, not to the edge.
threads.arc: From a floated import ban and a named distillation accusation, to a formal industry coalition letter with the frontier labs split, to the actual release landing before Washington resolves anything — the policy is now visibly chasing a technology that ships on its own timeline.

threads.name: Custom AI silicon vs Nvidia
threads.status: Kimi K3's MXFP4 four-bit format runs natively only on Nvidia Blackwell and AMD MI400, tying the largest open release directly to the two newest accelerator lines — reinforcing this week's AMD-Anthropic deal and the CUDA-moat deep dive that the contested asset is the software/hardware stack, not the model file.
threads.arc: As open models chase the frontier in size, the openness of the weights and the narrowness of the hardware that can run them advance together — 'more open' and 'less reachable' turn out to be the same motion.

dives.story: Kimi K3: the largest open model ever, and why 'open' no longer means local
dives.why_it_matters: Anyone weighing whether to adopt an open frontier model should internalize that at 2.8T parameters and 1.4TB in four-bit, the weights being free changes almost nothing for them — it takes ~18+ high-end accelerators just to load, runs only on Nvidia Blackwell / AMD MI400, and most 'adopters' will rent it; the openness buys host price-competition, data residency, and researcher access, not a model on your own machine.

dives.story: AREX: an answer is cheaper to check than to find
dives.why_it_matters: Anyone building agent systems should take the mechanism even if the benchmark numbers are generous: because verifying a candidate decomposes into cheap constraint-wise checks, spending compute on verify-and-retarget instead of regenerate lets a modest 122B/10B-active model match much larger frontier systems on deep-research tasks — the ablations (removing the outer loop drops BrowseComp 82.5->69.8) are the load-bearing evidence.
